lessons.title: Read your first C# program
lessons.subtitle: Familiar loops; a compiler checks types before execution.
rules: C# is the language. .NET supplies the runtime and libraries; the SDK supplies development tools; ASP.NET Core builds web apps.
A .csproj sets the target framework and dependencies. dotnet build compiles; dotnet run normally builds, then starts the app.
Main is the entry point. Top-level statements generate it; .NET 10 also supports file-based apps without a .csproj.
var infers one compile-time type. int, bool and string mean integer, Boolean and text; they are not interchangeable.
Arrays hold typed elements. foreach visits them. && requires both conditions; a single-statement body can omit braces.
lessons.pythonNote: Python lists can mix types and grow. This C# array has an element type and a fixed length.
lessons.trap: var does not mean Python-style rebinding to any type. Top-level code is still compiled C#.
lessons.agentConnection: Every generated app starts in Program.cs; its .csproj selects .NET and packages before request handling begins.

questions.prompt: What happens when this is compiled?

options.why: That would fit Python rebinding; C# has already inferred int for apples.

options.text: Compilation fails: apples is an int.
options.why: Correct. var selected int from 3; a later assignment cannot change that type.
var is compile-time inference. dynamic is a different, explicit C# feature.

questions.hint: The first assignment fixes the inferred type.
questions.explanation: The compiler rejects assigning a string to an int before this program can run.

questions.prompt: What type does the compiler infer for basket?

options.why: Correct. new[] creates an array and infers the element type int from these values.
A List<int> is a growable collection. new[] specifically creates an array.
Tuples use parentheses, such as (1, 2, 3), and are a different type.

questions.hint: The square brackets after new are the clue.
questions.explanation: new[] infers the element type. The resulting int[] has a fixed length of three.
questions.code: var basket = new[] { 1, 2, 3 };

questions.prompt: Fill one operator so both conditions must be true.
questions.hint: Use C# logical AND, which skips the right side when the left side is false.
questions.explanation: && is logical AND. The right condition is evaluated only when the left condition is true.

questions.prompt: Arrange these lines into a program that prints 4.
questions.hint: Each name must be declared before the line that uses it.
questions.explanation: The second line needs apples; the final line needs doubled. These data dependencies determine the order.

reference.meaning: <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk"><PropertyGroup><OutputType>Exe</OutputType><TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework><Nullable>enable</Nullable></PropertyGroup></Project> defines an executable project. Web projects use Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web.
These are the lesson targets. C# is versioned separately from .NET, and many demonstrated features existed before C# 14.
static void Main() is an explicit entry method inside a type. Alternatively, top-level statements appear before type declarations; only one project source file may contain top-level statements.
With .NET 10, dotnet run --file hello.cs builds and runs a standalone C# source file. The generated agents use projects; some development helpers can be file-based apps.
namespace Pantry; groups type names logically. A namespace need not equal a folder, though matching them often helps readers.
using System; lets you write Console instead of System.Console. It neither copies source nor installs a package. using for disposal is a separate syntax.
int count = 2; bool ready = true; string name = "Ada"; use explicit types. C# uses semicolons and braces; // starts a line comment.
while (count > 0) repeats while a condition stays true. continue skips to the next loop iteration; break exits the nearest loop. Make progress toward a stopping condition.

lessons.title: Functions, methods and little helpers
lessons.subtitle: Start with inputs and outputs; introduce objects only when needed.
rules: Read int Double(int number) as: returns int, named Double, accepts one int. void means no return value.
A static method belongs to its type; an instance method uses an object. A local function belongs inside another body.
Overloads share a name but differ in parameters. An override replaces an inherited virtual or abstract implementation.
number => number + extra is a lambda. Func<int, int> describes input and output types; captures can observe later changes.
out supplies an output; ref accesses an initialized caller variable; params accepts several arguments. Recursion needs a stopping case.
lessons.python:
extra = 2
add_extra = lambda number: number + extra
print(add_extra(3))
extra = 4
print(add_extra(3))
def double(number):
    return number * 2
print(double(3))
lessons.pythonNote: Both examples observe the later extra value. C# also checks the delegate signature; local functions can capture unless static.
lessons.trap: The arrow can introduce a lambda or an expression-bodied member. Neither makes the computation asynchronous.
lessons.agentConnection: Tool handlers are methods; routing and LINQ use lambdas. Small helpers can stay functions without new class hierarchies.

questions.prompt: What does the second Console.WriteLine print?

options.why: That is the first call. The lambda captured the variable, not a frozen copy of its original value.
Correct. extra is now 4, so addExtra(3) computes 3 + 4.

options.text: It fails because captured variables cannot change.
options.why: This captured local is mutable. A capture does not make it readonly.

questions.hint: Read the current value of extra when the lambda runs.
questions.explanation: The lambda reads the same captured variable on both calls; assigning 4 changes what the later call reads.

questions.prompt: What language feature is this pair of methods?

options.why: An override requires an inherited virtual or abstract member, and uses override.
Correct. The methods share a name but accept different parameter types.
Recursion happens when a function calls itself. Neither of these methods does.

questions.hint: Compare the parameter lists, not just the shared name.
questions.explanation: Overload selection uses the call arguments. string Repeat(string text) and int Repeat(int number) have distinct signatures.

questions.prompt: Fill one keyword so TryParse can assign its parsed result.
questions.code:
bool ok = int.TryParse("12", ___ var count);
Console.WriteLine(ok ? count : 0);
questions.hint: The method writes a result into this caller variable.
questions.explanation: out marks an output argument. TryParse assigns it and separately returns a bool indicating success; ref would require an initialized variable.

questions.prompt: What does Total(3) return?

options.why: The function adds n to a smaller recursive result; it does not return only the first n.
Correct. Total(3) is 3 + 2 + 1 + 0. n == 0 is the stopping case.
For this positive input, each call decreases n until it reaches zero.

questions.hint: Expand one call at a time until n reaches zero.
questions.explanation: The recursive calls return in reverse order: 0, then 1, then 3, then 6. This version is intended for nonnegative inputs.
questions.code:
static int Total(int n) => n == 0 ? 0 : n + Total(n - 1);
Console.WriteLine(Total(3));

reference.meaning: return value; sends a value back to the caller. Console.WriteLine(value) displays it. void means the function has no return value.
public static int Double(int number) { return number * 2; } is called as Helpers.Double(3) when declared in Helpers. Its expression-bodied equivalent ends with => number * 2;.
jar.Add(3) acts on jar. Inside an ordinary instance method, this denotes that current object; a static method has no this.
A helper declared inside a method or top-level body can use surrounding locals. Add static to forbid capturing surrounding instance or local state.
Func<int, int> accepts an int and returns an int. Action<int> accepts an int and returns void. A lambda supplies a callable value; => also appears in expression-bodied members.
int.TryParse(text, out var number) assigns number and returns a success bool. The caller does not have to initialize an out argument.

void Increment(ref int value) { value++; } can change a caller variable. Initialize int n = 2; then call Increment(ref n). Ordinary reference-type arguments already pass an object reference by value; ref is not needed to mutate that object.
static int Count(params int[] numbers) => numbers.Length; accepts Count(1, 2, 3) or Count(new[] { 1, 2, 3 }). params makes the last parameter accept a variable number of arguments.
A recursive helper calls itself on a smaller subproblem. A stopping case prevents endless calls; recursion is useful for nested structures, not a requirement for ordinary loops.
nameof(Double) produces the string "Double" at compile time when that symbol is in scope. It names the symbol without calling the function or reading its value.

lessons.title: Missing values without guessing
lessons.subtitle: A compiler warning helps; runtime checks still matter.
rules: null means absent, not empty text or zero. string? marks a nullable reference; int? can hold an integer or null.
<Nullable>enable</Nullable> enables reference annotations and compiler analysis. An annotation does not validate runtime input.
value?.Member accesses only when non-null; value ?? fallback uses the fallback only when value is null.
value! suppresses a compiler warning; it performs no runtime check. Prefer proving a value exists before using it.
is matches patterns: is null, is not null, or is "red" or "blue". && evaluates the right side only if needed.
lessons.python:
nickname = None
display = nickname if nickname is not None else "Guest"
print(display)
print(len(nickname) if nickname is not None else 0)
nickname = "Ada"
if nickname is not None and len(nickname) > 2:
    print("long enough")
lessons.pythonNote: Do not translate ?? as Python or: or also replaces empty strings, zero and other falsy values.
lessons.trap: name!.Length still throws if name is null. The exclamation mark changes compiler analysis, not the object.
lessons.agentConnection: Optional configuration and request properties need explicit defaults or validation before handlers dereference them.

questions.prompt: What does this print?

options.why: Correct. Empty text is a present string, so ?? keeps it.
?? replaces only null. It does not replace an empty string.
The left side is a valid string, and interpolation can print it.

questions.hint: Ask whether name is absent or merely empty.
questions.explanation: The fallback is skipped because name is not null. This differs from Python name or "Guest".
questions.code:
string? name = "";
Console.WriteLine($"[{name ?? "Guest"}]");

questions.prompt: Fill one operator to access Length only when name is non-null.
questions.code:
string? name = null;
Console.WriteLine(name___Length ?? 0);
questions.hint: This operator combines a null check with member access.
questions.explanation: ?. returns null here without accessing Length. ?? then supplies zero.

questions.prompt: Does this safely check whether name is long?

options.text: Yes; ! converts null into an empty string.
options.why: ! does not convert values or supply defaults.

options.text: No; ! suppresses a warning, and the access throws.
options.why: Correct. Runtime null remains null, so accessing Length throws NullReferenceException.

options.text: No; string? prevents the code from compiling.
options.why: Nullable annotations enable warnings, not a blanket ban on dereferencing.

questions.hint: The null-forgiving operator has no runtime effect.
questions.explanation: Use name is not null && name.Length > 3, or a suitable null-conditional expression, when absence is expected.
questions.code:
string? name = null;
bool isLong = name!.Length > 3;

questions.prompt: What does this print?

options.why: Correct. The first condition is false, so && skips the Length access.
The first condition is false because color is null.
Short-circuit && skips its right side when the left side is false.

questions.hint: Evaluate only the left condition first.
questions.explanation: The is not null pattern proves a value exists on the path where the right-hand expression runs.
questions.code:
string? color = null;
Console.WriteLine(color is not null && color.Length > 3);

reference.meaning: string? and string use the same runtime reference type; ? enables compiler analysis. int? is Nullable<int>, a value type that represents an integer or no value.
condition ? whenTrue : whenFalse selects one result. It is different from the nullable annotation in string? and the null-conditional operator ?. .
color is "red" or "blue" accepts either text value. count is >= 1 and <= 3 combines relational patterns; or/and here are pattern combinators, not ||/&& operators.
if (value is string text) proves value is a string and introduces text for the matching path. A property pattern can inspect shape: value is { Length: > 2 }.
name is not null && name.Length > 3 checks existence before accessing Length. Merely writing name! does not check anything at runtime.
name ??= "Guest" assigns "Guest" only if name is currently null. name ?? "Guest" merely produces a fallback value without assigning it to name.

lessons.title: An object is data with useful operations
lessons.subtitle: A class defines the shape; new creates one instance.
rules: A class is a type; new Jar(2) creates an instance. A constructor initializes each new object.
A field stores state. A property provides access; get reads, set assigns, and init restricts assignment to initialization.
Class primary-constructor parameters are inputs, not automatic public properties. Declare properties explicitly when callers need them.
public exposes; private confines to the type; internal confines to the assembly. static belongs to the type; sealed forbids subclassing.
readonly fields cannot be reassigned after their allowed initialization. Referenced objects may still mutate. Object initializers run after construction.
lessons.pythonNote: Python _count is a convention, unlike C# private. This Python label also lacks the C# init-only restriction.
lessons.trap: A primary constructor is shorter syntax for accepting construction inputs, not a second object or an automatic public API.
lessons.agentConnection: Stores and tool handlers keep state in fields and expose deliberate methods/properties; their constructors receive dependencies.

questions.prompt: After these lines, what does first.Count print?

options.why: second is not a copied Jar; both variables refer to the same object.
Correct. Assigning a class reference gives both variables access to the same Jar.

options.text: It fails because Jar is sealed.
options.why: sealed blocks subclasses; it does not prevent creating or mutating instances.

questions.hint: Count how many times new Jar appears.
questions.explanation: There is one Jar and two references. second.Add changes the object that first also refers to.

questions.prompt: With this complete class, can a caller read jar.start?

options.text: Yes; every primary parameter becomes a public property.
options.why: That property synthesis applies to positional records, not an ordinary class.

options.text: No; start is a constructor parameter, not a public member.
options.why: Correct. The class accepts start, but exposes no public property named start.
sealed only prevents inheritance; it does not change accessibility.

questions.hint: This is a class declaration without record.
questions.explanation: Add public int Start { get; } = start; if callers need a property. Parameters and properties are different structures.

questions.prompt: Fill one property accessor so assignment is allowed during initialization, but not later.
questions.hint: It is the initialization-only alternative to set.
questions.explanation: init permits new Jar { Label = "Rice" }. It does not permit jar.Label = "Beans" in an ordinary later statement.

questions.prompt: Using this Jar type, arrange the statements to create a jar, add three, then print the updated count.
questions.hint: Construction must precede using the object; print after its change.
questions.explanation: The constructor sets count to 2. Add changes it to 5. The final property read observes that updated state.

reference.meaning: class Jar { private int count; public Jar(int start) { count = start; } } spells out construction explicitly. Constructors use the type name and have no declared return type.
class Jar(int start) { private int count = start; } accepts the same input more concisely. start is a parameter, not a public property; it can be used within the type body.
private int count; is storage. public int Count => count; is a getter exposing that storage. public string Label { get; set; } is an auto-property with compiler-provided storage.
new Jar(2) { Label = "Rice" } constructs the object first, then assigns Label during initialization. required demands initialization by the caller; it does not validate the supplied value.
A readonly List<int> field cannot normally be reassigned outside field initialization or its declaring constructor, but its existing list can still Add elements.
A static field belongs to the type rather than one instance. Every instance can observe shared state through it; do not use it merely to avoid constructing an object.
An assembly is a compiled .dll or .exe unit. internal restricts ordinary access to that assembly; private restricts access to the declaring type, not the entire source file.
const int Limit = 5; declares a compile-time constant. A readonly field can instead be initialized at runtime during construction; neither keyword makes a referenced object deeply immutable.
A protected member is accessible within its declaring class and derived classes, subject to C# receiver rules. It is useful for base-class helpers; it is not publicly callable by any object.

lessons.title: Data shapes and copies
lessons.subtitle: Choose a simple shape; know what copying really copies.
rules: Class variables hold references; assigning one copies the reference. Struct assignment copies its value, including any references inside it.
record means record class unless struct is stated. Records generate value-based equality using their members’ equality rules.
Positional record-class parameters generate public init properties and deconstruction. Ordinary class primary parameters do not.
with copies a record and changes selected members. Nested reference objects remain shared: the copy is shallow.
Tuples group a few values: (string Name, int Count). Deconstruction, var (name, count), puts the components into local variables.
lessons.python:
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Label:
    color: str
    size: int
first = Label("Blue", 2)
same = Label("Blue", 2)
changed = replace(first, size=3)
print(first == same)
print(f"{first.size}/{changed.size}")
lessons.pythonNote: A frozen dataclass is a useful analogy, not an exact equivalent. It does not automatically support C# record-style deconstruction.
lessons.trap: Records are not deeply immutable. A record containing List<string> can share a mutable list, and list equality is not element equality.
lessons.agentConnection: Agent request/result records give data a clear shape. Readonly properties and with copies do not freeze nested lists.

questions.prompt: What does this print?

options.why: Correct. These Label records have the same type and equal Color and Size members.
Separate record instances can be equal because record equality compares their members.

options.text: It fails because == cannot compare records.
options.why: The compiler generates equality operators for records.

questions.hint: The declaration says record, not ordinary class.
questions.explanation: The generated equality compares member values here: strings compare their text, and integers compare their numeric value.
questions.code:
Console.WriteLine(new Label("Blue", 2) == new Label("Blue", 2));
record Label(string Color, int Size);

questions.prompt: What does this print after adding to the copy’s list?

options.why: with copied the record, not the nested List object. Both records still refer to the same list.
Correct. The shallow copy shares Items, so adding through copy changes the list original also holds.

options.text: It fails because records cannot contain mutable lists.
options.why: A record may hold a mutable collection. init-only prevents property reassignment, not changes inside that list.

questions.hint: Ask whether with also creates a new List here.
questions.explanation: The record objects differ, but their Items references point to the same list. Copy the list explicitly when independent contents are required.

questions.prompt: Fill one keyword to make a modified record copy.
questions.hint: This expression starts from the original record’s members.
questions.explanation: with creates the modified copy. first.Size remains 2; changed.Size becomes 3.

questions.prompt: What does this print?

options.why: Correct. Pair is a struct, so assigning a copies its value. Updating b.Count does not change a.Count.
That would be the result for this mutable shape declared as a class; here it is a value type.
b is mutable; changing its Count field succeeds and updates its own copy.

questions.hint: Find the struct keyword in the declaration.
questions.explanation: Value-type assignment copies the value. This example contains only an int; a struct can still contain references to shared objects.

reference.meaning: record Label(string Color, int Size) is a reference type with generated init properties. record struct Label(...) is a value type whose generated positional properties are normally mutable; readonly record struct makes them init-only.
Two records containing separate List<int> objects with equal elements are not automatically equal: each list normally uses reference equality. Records use the members’ own equality rules.
var snack = (Name: "Pear", Count: 2); var (name, count) = snack; creates local variables. Tuple labels aid readability; a tuple is not an interchangeable instance of a named record.
A copied record gets copied member values. Reference-valued members still point at the original nested objects unless explicitly replaced with fresh copies.

var snack = new { Name = "Pear", Count = 2 }; creates a compiler-generated type with read-only properties. new Jar { Label = "Rice" } instead initializes an existing named type. Both remain shallow with respect to referenced values.

lessons.title: Compose objects through small contracts
lessons.subtitle: An interface says what is available; an object does the work.
rules: An interface is a contract. IText inner accepts an existing implementing object; that parameter does not declare inheritance.
class PlainText : IText implements an interface. class Child : Parent inherits a base class: Child is a Parent.
A constructor dependency expresses has-a: Brackets has an IText. Passing it manually is dependency injection; a container is optional.
A decorator keeps the same contract, adds behavior, and forwards calls. virtual enables override; base accesses inherited behavior.
sealed blocks subclasses; sealed override blocks further overriding of that member. Keep simple transformations as functions when state is unnecessary.
lessons.pythonNote: This Python version relies on duck typing. C# explicitly checks the declared IText contract; neither needs a dependency-injection container.
lessons.trap: Implements, inherits and receives are three different relationships. A constructor parameter alone never means is-a.
lessons.agentConnection: Generated chat wrappers accept a client, add tracing or request behavior, and forward calls through a shared client contract.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Brackets here?

options.why: inner is a parameter naming an object, not a base class declaration.

options.text: Brackets implements IText and receives an IText dependency.
options.why: Correct. The colon states the contract; the constructor parameter receives another object satisfying it.

options.text: Brackets creates a new IText interface instance.
options.why: Interfaces are contracts. This constructor receives an already created implementation.

questions.hint: Read the parentheses and the colon separately.
questions.explanation: Brackets is usable as an IText and has an inner IText. Those are different relationships, joined by composition.

questions.prompt: What does this decorator pipeline print?

options.why: Both Brackets objects add behavior while forwarding; their output is not ignored.
There are two nested wrappers, and each contributes one pair of brackets.
Correct. The outer wrapper brackets the inner wrapper’s [hello] result.

questions.hint: Follow Read inward, then assemble its returned text outward.
questions.explanation: Each decorator calls its inner object once and wraps that result. This adds behavior without editing PlainText.

questions.prompt: Fill one keyword to replace the inherited virtual method.
questions.hint: This is the inheritance feature, not another method overload.
questions.explanation: override supplies the derived implementation. When an overridden virtual member is called, the runtime object type selects the implementation.

questions.prompt: You only need to convert Celsius to Fahrenheit. Which starting design is simplest?

options.text: A function accepting a number and returning a number.
options.why: Correct. No persistent object state or replaceable service is required by this task.

options.text: A base class plus a subclass for every temperature.
options.why: Individual numeric values do not require an inheritance hierarchy.

options.text: An interface, factory and dependency container before writing the formula.
options.why: Those tools can solve other needs, but this pure transformation does not need them.

questions.hint: Look for actual state or variation that would justify objects.
questions.explanation: Use the smallest structure that expresses the job: static double ToFahrenheit(double c) => c * 9 / 5 + 32. Add abstractions when a real need appears.

reference.meaning: new Brackets(new PlainText()) supplies a dependency through a constructor. A framework container may automate construction and lifetimes, but is not the definition of dependency injection.
class Friendly : Greeting { public override string Say() => base.Say() + "!"; } calls the base implementation, then adds behavior. The base method must permit overriding.
An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly. An abstract method declares a required implementation without a body; a concrete derived class must override it.
Keep interfaces small and tied to actual substitution needs. A pure calculation usually fits a function; an object is useful for associated state or interchangeable behavior.

lessons.title: Choose a container by its job
lessons.subtitle: The generic type tells you what goes inside.
rules: List<T> grows; T is the element type. Arrays have fixed length. Dictionary<TKey,TValue> maps keys; HashSet<T> keeps unique values.
IEnumerable<T> promises enumeration, not stored contents. IReadOnlyList<T> exposes indexing and Count without mutation methods through that interface.
A read-only interface does not freeze the underlying object or its elements. Another reference may still change them.
new() gets its type from context. [a, b] is a collection expression requiring a target type; new[] infers an array.
Extension methods are static methods callable with instance syntax. In a traditional declaration, this marks the first receiver parameter.
lessons.python:
fruit = ["pear", "plum", "pear"]
view = fruit
unique = set(fruit)
prices = {"pear": 2}
fruit.append("apple")
print(len(view))
print(len(unique))
print(prices["pear"])
lessons.pythonNote: The aliasing is similar. Python does not restrict view to IReadOnlyList operations; C# generic arguments are compiler-checked.
lessons.trap: IReadOnlyList<T> means this access path cannot mutate through that interface; it is not a deeply immutable snapshot.
lessons.agentConnection: Stores expose collections of records, use dictionaries for lookup and sets for deduplication, and pass enumeration contracts to helpers.

questions.prompt: Which type best expresses unique color names?

options.why: A list preserves elements including duplicates; uniqueness would need extra work.
Correct. A set enforces uniqueness according to its equality comparer.
That maps integers to integers; it does not express a set of text names.

questions.hint: The key requirement is uniqueness, not ordering or key-to-value lookup.
questions.explanation: HashSet<string> stores unique strings. Its comparer determines whether differently cased names count as equal.

questions.prompt: What does this print?

options.why: readOnly refers to the original list; it does not copy or freeze it.
Correct. The list changes through items, and the read-only interface observes the same object.
items is still a List<int>, so its mutation methods remain available.

questions.hint: There is only one list object in this example.
questions.explanation: IReadOnlyList hides mutation methods through that variable. It does not promise that every reference to the object is read-only.

questions.prompt: Fill one keyword to declare a traditional extension method receiver.
questions.hint: The parameter is still passed to a static method, but can appear before the dot at the call site.
questions.explanation: this marks the receiver parameter. "ha".Twice() can be written as TextExtras.Twice("ha"); the string class is not modified.

questions.prompt: Which declaration gives [] the target type it needs?

options.why: A collection expression has no standalone natural type for var to infer here.
Correct. The declared string[] supplies the target type for the collection expression.
The target element type int is incompatible with these string values.

questions.hint: The collection expression needs the destination collection type.
questions.explanation: Use string[] colors = [...], List<string> colors = [...], or var colors = new[] { ... }. The last form infers an array from new[].

reference.meaning: List<string> chooses string for the type parameter T. Dictionary<string, int> has two parameters: key type and value type. The angle brackets are type arguments, not comparisons.
if (prices.TryGetValue("pear", out var price)) uses a value only when its key exists. Direct prices["missing"] throws when the key is absent.
new HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase) treats "Red" and "red" as the same key. Choose this deliberately; default string comparison distinguishes them.
items[0] indexes; int[] items = [1, 2] creates a target-typed collection; items is [1, ..] tests a list pattern. Context changes the meaning of the same brackets.
List<int> values = new(); gets the construction type from the declaration. var values = new List<int>(); gets the variable type from the construction. var values = []; lacks the required target type.

lessons.title: A query is a recipe, not its results
lessons.subtitle: Track when iteration actually happens.
rules: Where filters; Any answers existence; Distinct removes duplicates; OrderByDescending sorts largest first. Comparers control equality or ordering where supplied.
FirstOrDefault returns the first item, or default(T): often null for references, zero for int. Default does not prove absence.
Many IEnumerable LINQ operations are deferred. foreach or a terminal operation executes the query; storing its variable does not cache results.
ToList and ToArray enumerate now and store a shallow snapshot. Re-enumerating a deferred query can repeat work and observe source changes.
Python generators also defer work, but a generator object is usually one-shot. A typical LINQ-to-Objects query can be enumerated again.
lessons.python:
sizes = [1, 3, 3]
def query():
    return dict.fromkeys(size for size in sizes if size > 1)
snapshot = list(query())
sizes.append(4)
print(",".join(map(str, sorted(query(), reverse=True))))
print(",".join(map(str, snapshot)))
print(bool(query()))
print(next(iter([]), 0))
lessons.pythonNote: The function creates a fresh query each call to mirror re-enumeration. A single stored Python generator would be consumed.
lessons.trap: Deferred does not mean async or background execution. Sorting still needs to examine its input when the query is enumerated.
lessons.agentConnection: Generated stores filter and rank local data with LINQ; materialization determines whether work repeats and which data version is observed.

questions.prompt: What does the final line print?

options.why: That was the count before the Add, but the deferred query was not stored as results then.
Correct. Count enumerates after 4 was added, so it finds 3 and 4.

options.text: It fails because Where returns no collection.
options.why: Where returns an enumerable query that Count can enumerate.

questions.hint: Find the operation that actually enumerates the query.
questions.explanation: Where stores the filtering recipe. Count executes it against the list as it exists at that time.

questions.prompt: Fill the LINQ method name to execute now and store a List<int>.
questions.code:
var values = new List<int> { 1, 3 };
List<int> saved = values.Where(x => x > 1).___();
questions.hint: It names the collection type requested on the left.
questions.explanation: ToList enumerates immediately and returns a new List<int>. Later structural changes to values do not change saved.

questions.prompt: What does FirstOrDefault return here?

options.why: The element type is int, whose default value is zero. int? would be a different element type.
Correct. default(int) is zero, so an empty integer sequence produces zero.

options.text: It throws because the sequence is empty.
options.why: First throws on an empty sequence; FirstOrDefault returns the default value.

questions.hint: The default comes from the element type, not the variable name.
questions.explanation: An empty int sequence and a sequence beginning with zero both produce zero here. Use an explicit presence check when that distinction matters.

reference.meaning: values.Select(x => x * 2) transforms each element when enumerated. Where selects which elements remain; Select chooses each result’s shape.
Any(predicate) stops after finding a match. Count(predicate) counts every match. Use Any when the question is only whether a match exists.
names.Distinct(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase) treats differently cased versions as duplicates. The default string comparer treats them as different.
Changing a List before a later enumeration can change query results. Changing it while an active enumerator is traversing it may throw; a list is not a concurrent snapshot.
FirstOrDefault() returns null for an empty string sequence but 0 for an empty int sequence. First() throws instead; modern overloads can also accept an explicit fallback.
